similarity_meaning_real_values.text: Each Earth point is paired with its lunar twin: the 1-degree lunar cell, inside the mission's target zone, whose real values are closest. Similarity is computed on real values within stated tolerances: every key variable of the twin is within its tolerance of the Earth point and every secondary variable within twice its tolerance, and each variable scores lower the further apart the two values are. Each mission has its own score rule. Solar panels: the score falls from 1 with the first difference, as exp(-0.5 (difference / tolerance)^2). Rover: a difference within the measurement uncertainty of the elevation models (slope 0.27 degrees, roughness 17.4 m) scores 1, and beyond it the score falls as exp(-0.5 max(0, difference / uncertainty - 1)^2). Both values and their difference are shown side by side.

similarity_meaning_lunar_base.text: Each Earth point is paired with its lunar twin: the 1-degree cell, among NASA's nine candidate landing regions near the lunar south pole, that holds the same thermal position and has a similar terrain. The coldest temperature and the daily temperature swing are compared as positions: where the point ranks among Earth's lunar-base candidates against where its twin ranks among the cells of the nine regions, each within 10 percentile points; the two places are not equally cold and the real values are far apart. Slope and roughness are compared in real values (the twin within 4 degrees and 60 m). The real values on both sides and their differences are shown next to every pair.

Tenths in JavaScript: const s = f32Decimal(raw).toFixed(12), i = s.indexOf('.'); A = Number(s.slice(0, i)) * 10 + Number(s[i + 1]) + (Number(s[i + 2]) >= 5 ? 1 : 0). The 2-degree arc is 222.390 km with 6,371.0 and 222.390 km with 6,371.0088 (0.3 m apart; 222.4 km at the published precision). Over the 180 latitudes the sunlight above the atmosphere differs by at most 0.00012 kWh per square metre per day (it moves the 4th published decimal on 68 latitudes, never the 3rd); no number entering a result was changed.

rover_suitability_saturation.text: The Rover suitability is saturated too. 250 of the 254 sites tied at the top score the maximum on every one of the team's Rover criteria (slope (degrees) 45 %, full marks at 1 or less; roughness (m) 30 %, full marks at 30 or less; bare-ground share 25 %, full marks at 0.7 or more), so the team's criteria do not tell them apart either (253 of the 10,337 ranked points show a suitability of 100.00). Points that reach the maximum of each criterion, among the 10,337 ranked: slope (degrees) 3,291; roughness (m) 2,144; bare-ground share 930; all three: 250. Among the 254 tied sites: slope 0.500 to 0.961 degrees, roughness 14.61 to 30.19 m, bare-ground share 0.707 to 1.000. Worked example: Bardenas Reales (number 7,046, similarity 100.00, suitability 70.43): slope (degrees) 1.91, utility 0.93, 2.9 points lost; roughness (m) 77, utility 0.92, 2.3 points lost; bare-ground share 0.0176, utility 0.03, 24.4 points lost; Tabernas Desert (number 7,390, similarity 100.00, suitability 69.36): slope (degrees) 3.17, utility 0.85, 7.0 points lost; roughness (m) 111, utility 0.87, 3.9 points lost; bare-ground share 0.146, utility 0.21, 19.8 points lost; against the first analog shown (number 3, similarity 100.00, suitability 100.00): slope (degrees) 0.77, utility 1.00, 0.0 points lost; roughness (m) 29.3, utility 1.00, 0.0 points lost; bare-ground share 0.868, utility 1.00, 0.0 points lost. The criteria as the team wrote them reward the gentlest, barest ground and say nothing else about mobility (a recognised badlands analog with some vegetation cover loses about a quarter of its score on the bare-ground share alone); this is a weakness of the suitability criteria, left as written and to be examined by the re-audit.
